reason: Both are accurate against facts.md (5 of 14 for the prefix gate, 0 of 14 / 8 of 8 for scoped and approval bound, read only 4 of 8, the ceiling-by-design and untested-hardlink caveats). B is the better Khan-style interactive lesson: its step-2 quiz and the five-trick deck in step 3 take a guess, say 'Right' or 'Not quite' and explain, then animate a walk of the path through the map; step 4 lets the reader pick or type any path and see the starts-with gate and the safer gate decide side by side with reasons (editing a path to tmp/../output/x.txt correctly flips the verdicts); step 5's scoreboard squares open the real request ID and decision. A is a polished single-screen chalkboard replay that would make a cleaner GIF, but its one 'Your turn' quiz removes the answer buttons after about 5 seconds, auto-reveals the answer at about 10 s, and gives no feedback on the reader's pick, so the interaction is mostly decorative. B's step 6 also explains why 5 of 14 is a list of tricks rather than a failure rate, which A only implies.

A: Step 3 'Your turn' quiz: answer buttons disappear after ~5 s and the answer auto-reveals; clicking a choice gives no right/wrong feedback on what the reader picked.
Interaction is thin: step 4 trick cards only replay fixed animations, and the safer gate is never tried on a reader-chosen path; it is closer to an autoplay replay than an interactive lesson.
At 390 px each step leaves a large empty band between the explanation and the controls, and long paths (step 3-5) run to the card edge in a stylised font that is harder to read.
B: Several steps (the rules map, the trick walk, the playground, the scoreboard) are taller than a phone screen, and a sticky 'Tap a square' panel plus the fixed Back/Next bar cover a large part of the viewport while scrolling.
The step-2 quiz uses the same tmp-other look-alike case that reappears as trick 1 in step 3, so the reader answers it twice.
Text-heavy, long multi-panel steps would be hard to turn into the LinkedIn GIF the requester mentioned; the 'Write a report' path (output/summary.txt) is illustrative but not labelled as such.
